preamble: Voicing of the voiceless dental fricative [θ] to [ð] is well documented in Germanic. Under Verner's law, Proto-Germanic *θ from Grimm's law became *ð when the preceding syllable was unstressed; Old Norse voiced *θ medially and finally, keeping þ [θ] only word-initially; early Middle English voiced the initial /θ/ of unstressed function words such as the and thou. In Castilian Spanish /θ/ is voiced before a voiced consonant. Laklãnõ (Xokleng, Southern Jê) voiced Proto-Southern Jê *θ to ð, as in ðy 'to weave' against Kaingang ɸy.

examples.note: The fricative was voiced because the accent fell after it; compare *brōþēr 'brother' with root accent, which kept *θ.
Accent on the following syllable triggered voicing, as in *fadēr.
Medial *θ became [ð]; compare Gothic broþar and Old English brōþor.
Final *θ became [ð]; compare Gothic airþa and Old English eorþe.
Initial /θ/ of frequent unstressed function words became /ð/ in early Middle English, creating pairs such as thigh : thy.
The same voicing affected other unstressed function words beginning with þ.
/θ/ is voiced before a voiced consonant; voiced and voiceless realizations alternate freely.
The voicing applies across a word boundary before /n/.
Kaingang has ɸy. After a nasal the fricative did not voice (*ŋ.θ > k.θ).

sources: Wikipedia contributors (2026). Pronunciation of English th. https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pronunciation_of_English_th
Nikulin, A. (2020). Proto-Macro-Jê: um estudo reconstrutivo. https://repositorio.unb.br/handle/10482/38893
